paper_metadata.title: Seizure recurrence after a 1st unprovoked seizure: An extended follow-up

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study used a robust surveillance system to identify patients at the point of first medical contact, minimizing referral bias. Inclusion/exclusion criteria were highly specific and the baseline characteristics were well-defined.

items.label: Source of target population
items.prompt: The source population or population of interest is adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: This comprised review of hospital admissions, referrals to EEG laboratories, and referrals to the neurology and epilepsy clinics at 4 hospitals affiliated with the University of Minnesota.
items.reasoning: The authors clearly define the geographic and institutional source of the population.

items.label: Method used to identify population
items.prompt: The sampling frame and recruitment are adequately described, including methods to identify the sample sufficient to limit potential bias (number and type used, e.g., referral patterns in health care)
items.evidence_snippet: Potential cases of 1st seizure were ascertained through a surveillance system to identify patients presenting for evaluation of newly identified seizures.
items.reasoning: The use of a multi-hospital surveillance system at the point of first contact helps mitigate the 'referral bias' common in specialty clinic studies.

items.label: Recruitment period
items.prompt: Period of recruitment is adequately described
items.evidence_snippet: followed prospectively a total of 853 person-years... through 1985.
items.reasoning: While the end date of follow-up is mentioned (1985), the specific start date for the recruitment of this extended cohort is not explicitly stated, though it follows an earlier report.

items.label: Place of recruitment
items.prompt: Place of recruitment (setting and geographic location)  are adequately described
items.evidence_snippet: at 4 hospitals affiliated with the University of Minnesota.
items.reasoning: The setting is clearly identified as a specific academic hospital network.

items.label: Inclusion and exclusion criteria
items.prompt: Inclusion and exclusion criteria are adequately described (e.g., including explicit diagnostic criteria or “zero time” description).
items.evidence_snippet: The subjects of this report are restricted to those who (1) had experienced a definite unprovoked seizure as documented by an eyewitness, (2) on review of past history had not experienced a previous unprovoked seizure, and (3) were identified and had signed consent forms within 24 hours of the index seizure.
items.reasoning: Criteria are very specific, including a 'zero time' requirement of 24 hours from the index event.

items.label: Adequate study participation
items.prompt: There is adequate participation in the study by eligible individuals
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: The text does not provide the total number of eligible patients who declined to participate (participation rate), only the number of those who signed consent.

items.label: Baseline characteristics
items.prompt: The baseline study sample (i.e., individuals entering the study) is adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: The patient's seizures were categorized by etiology as idiopathic... or remote symptomatic... All seizures were categorized as partial or generalized onset.
items.reasoning: Key prognostic variables like etiology, seizure type, and EEG findings are described for the baseline sample.

quips_assessment.goal: Goal: To judge the risk of attrition bias (likelihood that relationship between PF and outcome are different for completing and non-completing participants).
quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The attrition rate was relatively low (approx 15%), and the authors noted that most dropouts contributed significant follow-up time. Reasons for withdrawal were documented.

items.label: Proportion of baseline sample available for analysis
items.prompt: Response rate (i.e., proportion of study sample completing the study and providing outcome data) is adequate.
items.evidence_snippet: Although 31 patients were lost to follow-up, almost all contributed at least 2 years to the analyses.
items.reasoning: 31/208 (14.9%) is a reasonable attrition rate for a long-term follow-up study, and person-years were utilized.

items.label: Attempts to collect information on participants who dropped out
items.prompt: Attempts to collect information on participants who dropped out of the study are described.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: The study does not describe specific efforts to trace or re-engage those lost to follow-up.

items.label: Reasons and potential impact of subjects lost to follow-up
items.prompt: Reasons for loss to follow-up are provided.
items.evidence_snippet: A total of 20 subjects were withdrawn because of death (8), an intervening CNS insult such as head trauma thought to increase the risk for seizures (8), or patient request to terminate our follow-up contacts (4).
items.reasoning: Specific reasons for withdrawal are categorized.

items.label: Outcome and prognostic factor information on those lost to follow-up
items.prompt: Participants lost to follow-up are adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: The paper does not provide a comparison of baseline characteristics between those who completed the study and those lost to follow-up.

items.prompt: There are no important differences between key characteristics (LIST) and outcomes in participants who completed the study and those who did not.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: Without a comparison table or statistical test, it is impossible to determine if attrition was informative (biased).

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: Study Attrition Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: Loss to follow-up (from baseline sample to study population analyzed) is not associated with key characteristics (i.e., the study data adequately represent the sample) sufficient to limit potential bias to the observed relationship between PF and outcome.

quips_assessment.goal: Goal: To judge the risk of measurement bias related to how PF was measured (differential measurement of PF related to the level of outcome).
quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: Prognostic factors were defined using international standards (ILAE) and measured at baseline, preventing knowledge of the outcome from influencing the measurement.

items.label: Definition of the PF
items.prompt: A clear definition or description of 'PF' is provided (e.g., including dose, level, duration of exposure, and clear specification of the method of measurement).
items.evidence_snippet: Five categories of EEG findings were evaluated: (1) generalized spike and wave (GSW) patterns... (2) focal epileptiform... (3) focal slowing... (4) nonspecific slowing... and (5) normal.
items.reasoning: The PFs (EEG, etiology, Todd's paresis) are explicitly defined.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of PF
items.prompt: Method of PF measurement is adequately valid and reliable to limit misclassification bias (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and limited reliance on recall).
items.evidence_snippet: All seizures were categorized as partial or generalized onset based upon description of the seizure by an eyewitness according to criteria recommended by the ILAE.
items.reasoning: Standardized ILAE criteria were used, and the 24-hour recruitment window minimized recall bias.

items.prompt: Continuous variables are reported or appropriate cut-points (i.e., not data-dependent) are used.
items.evidence_snippet: Age was analyzed both as a continuous and as a discrete variable.
items.reasoning: The authors avoided arbitrary cut-points for age.

items.label: Method and Setting of PF Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of measurement of PF is the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: Interviews were scheduled to obtain medical (and especially neurologic) history, as well as family and social history.
items.reasoning: A standardized interview protocol was applied to all participants.

items.label: Proportion of data on PF available for analysis
items.prompt: Adequate proportion of the study sample has complete data for PF variable.
items.evidence_snippet: 208 were identified with a 1st unprovoked seizure, recruited within 24 hours, and had their interviews completed within 30 days.
items.reasoning: The strict inclusion criteria ensured that all 208 analyzed patients had the required baseline PF data.

items.label: Method used for missing data
items.prompt: Appropriate methods of imputation are used for missing 'PF' data.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: Imputation was not mentioned; however, the study design likely resulted in very little missing baseline data.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: PF Measurement Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: PF is adequately measured in study participants to sufficiently limit potential bias.

quips_assessment.goal: Goal: To judge the risk of bias related to the measurement of outcome (differential measurement of outcome related to the baseline level of PF).
quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: While the outcome (seizure recurrence) is clearly defined, it relies on patient/parent report during 6-12 month intervals, which may be subject to recall bias, and there is no mention of blinding the outcome assessors to the baseline PFs.

items.label: Definition of the Outcome
items.prompt: A clear definition of outcome is provided, including duration of follow-up and level and extent of the outcome construct.
items.evidence_snippet: The cumulative risks of recurrence were determined by life-table methods, with event defined as an unprovoked seizure recurrence.
items.reasoning: The outcome is clearly defined as the occurrence of a second unprovoked seizure.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of Outcome
items.prompt: The method of outcome measurement used is adequately valid and reliable to limit misclassification bias (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and confirmation of outcome with valid and reliable test).
items.evidence_snippet: Subjects were contacted at 6-month intervals for 2 years from date of the 1st seizure and annually thereafter through 1985.
items.reasoning: Outcome relies on self-report/interview. While standard in epilepsy research, there is no mention of blinding the interviewers to the patient's baseline risk factors (e.g., EEG results).

items.label: Method and Setting of Outcome Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of outcome measurement is the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: Subjects were contacted at 6-month intervals for 2 years from date of the 1st seizure and annually thereafter through 1985.
items.reasoning: The follow-up schedule was standardized for the entire cohort.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: Outcome Measurement Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: Outcome of interest is adequately measured in study participants to sufficiently limit potential bias.

quips_assessment.goal: Goal: To judge the risk of bias due to confounding (i.e. the effect of PF is distorted by another factor that is related to PF and outcome).
quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study used multivariable Cox proportional hazards models to adjust for potential confounders, including etiology and EEG findings.

items.label: Important Confounders Measured
items.prompt: All important confounders, including treatments (key variables in conceptual model: LIST), are measured.
items.evidence_snippet: Possible risk factors... included abnormal neurologic examination, abnormal EEG other than GSW, status epilepticus or multiple seizures, age, gender, seizure type, Todd's paresis, history of epilepsy in parents, and history of acute symptomatic seizures.
items.reasoning: A comprehensive list of clinical and demographic confounders was collected.

items.label: Definition of the confounding factor
items.prompt: Clear definitions of the important confounders measured are provided (e.g., including dose, level, and duration of exposures).
items.evidence_snippet: The patient's seizures were categorized by etiology as idiopathic... or remote symptomatic (seizures in individuals with a prior history of CNS insult known to substantially increase the risk for subsequent epilepsy, such as head trauma, cerebrovascular insult, CNS infection, or static encephalopathy).
items.reasoning: Confounders like etiology were rigorously defined.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of Confounders
items.prompt: Measurement of all important confounders is adequately valid and reliable (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and limited reliance on recall).
items.evidence_snippet: Potential misclassification... was evaluated by comparing hospital records with study interview forms for a random sample.
items.reasoning: The authors performed a validation sub-study to ensure the reliability of their history-taking.

items.label: Method and Setting of Confounding Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of confounding measurement are the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: Interviews were scheduled to obtain medical (and especially neurologic) history, as well as family and social history.
items.reasoning: Standardized for all participants.

items.label: Method used for missing data
items.prompt: Appropriate methods are used if imputation is used for missing confounder data.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: No imputation methods were described.

items.label: Appropriate Accounting for Confounding
items.prompt: Important potential confounders are accounted for in the study design (e.g., matching for key variables, stratification, or initial assembly of comparable groups).
items.evidence_snippet: Different predictors of recurrence were identified in those with remote symptomatic seizures when compared with those with idiopathic seizures, so results of Kaplan-Meier analyses are presented separately.
items.reasoning: The authors used stratification by etiology to handle the most significant confounder.

items.prompt: Important potential confounders are accounted for in the analysis (i.e., appropriate adjustment).
items.evidence_snippet: The proportional hazards model was used to estimate univariate and multivariate rate ratios.
items.reasoning: Multivariable Cox regression was used to adjust for multiple factors simultaneously.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: Study Confounding Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: Important potential confounders are appropriately accounted for, limiting potential bias with respect to the relationship between PF and outcome.

quips_assessment.goal: Goal: To judge the risk of bias related to the statistical analysis and presentation of results.
quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The statistical methods (Life-table, Kaplan-Meier, Cox regression) are appropriate for time-to-event data. The reporting is transparent, including both univariate and multivariate results.

items.label: Presentation of analytical strategy
items.prompt: There is sufficient presentation of data to assess the adequacy of the analysis.
items.evidence_snippet: The cumulative risks of recurrence were determined by life-table methods... Univariate analysis (Kaplan-Meier survival curves)... The proportional hazards model was used to estimate univariate and multivariate rate ratios.
items.reasoning: The analytical plan is standard and well-described.

items.label: Model development strategy
items.prompt: The strategy for model building (i.e., inclusion of variables in the statistical model) is appropriate and is based on a conceptual framework or model.
items.evidence_snippet: When all factors significant in the univariate analysis were entered into a multivariate Cox analysis (table 1), the same predictors... remained significant.
items.reasoning: The strategy of moving from univariate significance to a multivariate model is a standard approach.

items.prompt: The selected statistical model is adequate for the design of the study.
items.evidence_snippet: The proportional hazards model was used to estimate univariate and multivariate rate ratios.
items.reasoning: Cox proportional hazards is the gold standard for prognostic studies with varying follow-up times.

items.label: Reporting of results
items.prompt: There is no selective reporting of results.
items.evidence_snippet: Table 1. Univariate rate ratios and multivariate rate ratios (95% confidence intervals) as estimated by Cox regression analysis
items.reasoning: The authors report both significant and non-significant findings for all variables tested.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: Statistical Analysis and Presentation Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: The statistical analysis is appropriate for the design of the study, limiting potential for presentation of invalid or spurious results.
